title: Indian-American Donors Give Republicans Four-to-One Funding Edge Ahead of Midterms
excerpt: FEC-based analyses put Republican-linked giving at $15.8 million against $3.7 million for Democrats, led by Asha Jadeja Motwani and Michelle D'Souza, even as Indian-American voters lean Democratic.
body:
• Indian-American donors have given $15.8 million to Republican-linked PACs since 2025 against $3.7 million to Democrats, a roughly 4-to-1 edge, according to a Hindustan Times analysis of FEC data reported by Inshorts.
  • Venture capitalist Asha Jadeja Motwani is the largest named donor at about $5.9 million in that analysis; defence contractor chief executive Michelle D'Souza gave more than $4 million.
  • A separate FEC review of 11 prominent donors put the split at about $10.8 million to Republicans and $3.3 million to Democrats — the samples differ, but both point the same way.
  • For readers: the donor elite is not the electorate — the 2026 AAPI Voter Survey found Indian-American voters backing Democratic Senate candidates 66 to 18.

Indian-American big donors are giving Republicans a large funding edge ahead of the November midterms, even as Indian-American voters continue to lean Democratic. An analysis of Federal Election Commission data reported by Inshorts, citing Hindustan Times, put contributions to Republican-linked PACs since 2025 at $15.8 million, against $3.7 million to Democrats — a roughly four-to-one advantage for President Donald Trump's party.

The two largest names in that analysis are venture capitalist Asha Jadeja Motwani, at about $5.9 million, and entrepreneur and defence contractor chief executive Michelle D'Souza, at more than $4 million. D'Souza's $4 million to Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., was also recorded in The Hill's review of end-of-year campaign finance filings, which listed her among MAGA Inc.'s largest backers over the past year.

Two counts, one direction

The exact ratio depends on which donors and committees are counted. A separate review of FEC filings for 11 prominent donors, reported by IANS on October 19, found about $10.8 million in direct gifts to Republican committees and groups against about $3.3 million to Democrats — roughly three to one. That review said about $7.1 million of the Republican total came in three checks to MAGA Inc. from Motwani, Krishna Tripuraneni and Anjani Sinha, and put Motwani's direct giving above $7 million in total, including $5.1 million to MAGA Inc. and $886,000 to the Republican National Committee.

https://x.com/htTweets/status/2113816553724707231

Both analyses carry the same caveat: they cover samples of named, prominent donors, not all Indian-American giving. VoterAtlas, a site that matches FEC donors against Indian and South Asian surnames, counted $35.3 million in itemised 2026-cycle receipts through August 30, without a party split.

The Democratic side of the ledger

The largest Indian-American Democratic donor in the IANS review remains venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, with about $2.1 million, almost all of it to Senate Majority PAC. The Impact Fund, the political arm of Indian American Impact, has raised about $1.92 million this cycle and held about $331,000 in cash on hand at September 30, according to FEC filings cited in the review. Its largest gift was $500,000 from WestBridge Capital's Sumir Chadha.

Some Republican money from these donors has also reached opponents of Indian-American Democrats. The review said the House Republican joint fundraising committee Grow the Majority passed $7,000 each from Motwani's and Palantir executive Shyam Sankar's gifts to Jay Feely, who faces Democrat Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st District, while a $3,500 share of a gift in Sankar's name went to Casey Askar, the opponent of Pia Dandiya in Florida's 22nd District.

Donors and voters are moving differently

The giving pattern sits in sharp contrast to how the community votes. The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey found Indian-American voters backing Democratic Senate candidates by 66 to 18, though the review noted the survey's Indian-American sample is small. That gap — a wealthy, increasingly Republican donor class inside a still heavily Democratic electorate — is the central political fact for diaspora readers watching the midterms: campaign money and community votes are, for now, telling two different stories.

What to watch next is whether the late-cycle filings widen or narrow the gap, and whether Democratic groups can convert the community's voter lean into comparable large-donor fundraising before November.
